title: If a human approves every automated recommendation without ever deviating, are we actually providing human review?
description: A board-level oversight question testing whether a nominal human-review safeguard on an automated scoring system is genuine, using the observable deviation rate as the test rather than the existence of a review step on paper.
question_text: What is the deviation rate between our automated scores and the human reviewer's final decision — and if it is at or near zero, are we prepared for a regulator to conclude, as the CJEU did for SCHUFA-style scoring, that the score itself is making the decision?
rationale: The CJEU's SCHUFA ruling means an automated score can trigger GDPR Article 22 obligations even when a human formally makes the final call, if that human's review is not meaningful. A near-zero deviation rate is direct, observable evidence the review may be symbolic.
follow_up_actions: Request the current human deviation rate log for every scored decision process.
If the deviation rate is near zero, ask whether reviewers have the authority, time, and information to genuinely disagree.
Confirm legal has assessed GDPR Article 22 exposure in light of the SCHUFA ruling.

citations.title: Judgment of the Court (First Chamber), 7 December 2023 — OQ v Land Hessen (SCHUFA Holding, Scoring), Case C-634/21
citations.publisher: Court of Justice of the European Union
